course.title: Senior Project in Geology
course.description: Senior Project.Field-, laboratory- or library-based geological research to address an original question undertaken by arrangement with a faculty supervisor during the senior year. Students conducting field or laboratory research generally start their work in the summer prior to their senior year. Half-course each semester. Grade and credit awarded at the end of the second semester. (Students may complete the thesis in one semester by permission.) Letter grade only.

course.title: Africa After the End of History
course.description: This one-time seminar/course is connected to the international symposium of the same title scheduled for October 22-23, 2026, at Pomona College.  This symposium will bring about 12-15 US and international Africanist scholars to present and discuss the extent to which changing international conditions are affecting the continent.  Students in this course will mix conventional and experiential learning, help organize and run the symposium, interact with participants, and present their own research at poster sessions during the symposium.  Class meetings before the conference will focus on reading and discussing scholarship on the conference topics including the essay of the participants.  Class meetings after the conference are a mix of the above, and collective editing and arranging of symposium presentations into an edited volume or special issue of a journal.  No prerequisite.  Introduction to Comparative Politics and Comparative Politics of Africa will prepare students well.

course.title: Economics of Immigration
course.description:
This course applies an economic lens to the controversial and much debated topic of im-
migration. Issues covered include the decision to migrate, the effects of immigration on
markets, public finance, and income inequality, and the implications of immigration policies
in a global context. The course aims to enable informed opinions on immigration issues
based on cogent arguments, empirical evidence, and economic analyses.

course.title: Intermediate Media Projects
course.description: This is a topic-driven, intermediate-level production course. Topics are chosen in response to student interest in particular areas of media theory, or to enable them to adapt to ever changing platforms of media technology.  Students in the class will develop specialized technical skills based on their training in introductory production courses and focus on specific fields of knowledge within Media Studies.

course.title: Animation: Art and Motion
course.description:
Animation: Art and Motion
This production course is an introduction to experimental animation techniques. Through screenings, readings and hands-on activities and assignments, students will develop a vocabulary and methodology of the fundamentals of frame-by-frame movement and motion. Particular focus will be given to animated works that are created outside of the industry, and students will develop a critical understanding of animation as a medium in conversation with other forms of art.

course.title: Cinematography
course.description: This course is an introduction to cinematography. Through a hands-on, problem-solving-oriented approach, students will learn how to give shape to the images that they have in their minds. Students will learn the fundamentals of exposure, camera lenses and sensors, framing and composition, lighting, and rigging. Since film is not made in a vacuum, students will also gain knowledge relating to film history and its movements through the screening of feature and short films to learn how other filmmakers make use of cinematography and its tools. Students with limited knowledge on cameras, lights, and lenses are strongly encouraged to enroll.

course.title: Senior Thesis in History
course.description: Fall enrollment for a one-semester thesis, or a two-semester thesis. Enroll for HIST192 SC in the spring for a two-semester thesis.

course.title: Senior Thesis in English
course.description: Scripps senior English majors who are taking one of the seminars eligible for the senior requirement (course number ending in S) are concurrently enrolled in this course as well. ENGL199T SC refers to the 30-page thesis that emerges from those seminars. Fall or spring, depending on the senior seminar. Formerly ENGL191

course.title: Selected Topic in Dance (Studio)
course.description:
Course topics under this number will vary from year to year. This course explores a current topic in dance/dance studies with an emphasis on physical practice and the history and socio-cultural politics that frame that practice. Areas of study may include South and North American, Asian, European, and African Diaspora dance plus courses in alternative techniques and somatic-based training for the body. Consult Schedule of Classes for topic to be offered in a specific term. May be repeated for credit with different topics. Permission of instructor required. Full credit.

Topic for Spring 2020 - Intermediate Hip-Hop/House:  This full credit course will provide students with the opportunity to physically practice, rehearse, and improvise Hip-Hop and House dance. Geared to dancers at the Intermediate level and higher, the course will also include the study of historical, cultural, and aesthetic issues that underpin the movement practice.

Does not satisfy the foreign language requirement. Limited to one enrollment per semester and a cumulative total of one course credit.

course.title: Death, Dying, and the Afterlife
course.description: This course will explore various ways East Asian religious traditions deal with death and the dead. We will examine how the Daoist, Buddhist, and folk traditions of East Asia historically and currently address the question of "What happens when we die?" We will look at different ritual practices surrounding death, dying and the dead in their ongoing relationships with the living. We will also explore various descriptions of the terrain of the afterlife or postmortem world by critically engaging a variety of textual and visual records of China, Korea and Japan. Some of the topics that will be discussed in the course include the nature of the self, the function of funerary rites, the geography of the afterlife, communication with the dead and religious notions of salvation/liberation. By exploring a variety of narratives and practices regarding death and the afterlife, students will develop a rich and detailed picture of the relationship between the living and the dead in the East Asian religious landscape.

course.title: Psychology and Law
course.description: Examines psychological assumptions and interpersonal processes in the American legal system. Issues such as police interrogation, plea bargains, jury selection, eyewitness identification, attorney persuasion tactics, forensic science, jury decision-making, lie detection, the insanity defense, the effectiveness of prisons, and the death penalty are analyzed from a social-psychological perspective. Emphasis is on how research findings can be used to enhance the gathering of evidence, improve legal decision making, reduce crime, and promote justice. Previously PSYC188 CM.

course.title: Calculus II
course.description:
Transcendental functions, techniques of integration, infinite series,
related topics and applications. Again, each concept will be treated from numerical,
analytic and geometric perspectives. Prerequisite: A grade of C or above in
Mathematics 30 or placement exam.

course.title: Calculus III
course.description:
Vectors and vector functions, partial derivatives and differentiability
of functions of several variables, multiple integrals. Prerequisite: Mathematics 31 or
equivalent, or placement score.

course.title: Undocumented Organizing in LA
course.description: Undocumented L.A. is a class about organizing and historical memory.  It will explore the unrecorded and undocumented history of community and labor organizing efforts in Los Angeles. Students will study and analyze different forms of or approaches to organizing and various campaigns in LA from late 20th Century to the present.  Students will explore theories and conceptions of organizing, social change, and social movements. At the same time students will explore how to document organizing and roles of often overlooked social actors, such as Central Americans, Afro-Latines, queer and Transgender communities, women, Asian, BIPOC, multiracial communities. Students will examine intersections across lines of difference and institutional positioning and will learn how to construct inclusive histories and consider their relevance to current struggles. Students will conduct oral histories, review historical materials, newspapers and other sources to help construct memories for organizations and individuals or to document a movement that has received little attention in the history books.

course.title: Policy and Race
course.description: This course examines the interplay between race and policy in recent US history primarily through the prism of the modern Black experience. Race is also experienced differently in terms of class and gender, which we will discuss throughout this course. In this way, this course considers the past, present, and future of policies informing race, gender, and class.

course.title: International Money and Finance
course.description: In global financial markets the foreign exchange market, and therefore the exchange rate, forms an integral part of the financial system and the most important price in any economy. The choice of exchange rate policy is particularly important for open economies, in which the relationship between domestic and international economies affect virtually all other economic conditions. In particular, the decision to enter a monetary union can bring important economic benefits as well as costs for the member countries. Because monetary unions are a form of regional integration and because regional integration is important in global politics the decision to join a monetary union needs to be analyzed in the political economy arena as well. This course will give a brief introduction to the historical, economic and political process associated with monetary unions and will cover this topic from an inter-disciplinary perspective.

course.title: Case Studies Sustainable Blt Env
course.description: Oral, drawn, photographed, and written analytical and projective (re)presentations of built projects and cases in digital forms of various types - individual and group work will be peer and outside-critic evaluated and graded in a series of assigned exercises.

course.title: Introduction to Psychology
course.description: The purpose of the course is to introduce the student to psychology as it developed from a nonscientific interest to a scientific approach to human behavior. Special attention will be given to some of the major systems, issues and methods involved in contemporary psychology. Students will be expected to participate in research studies in psychology or complete an approved alternative.

course.title: Community Health
course.description: This course explores the struggle for social justice and health equality for and with underserved Asian American communities and Pacific Islander communities. Through participatory teaching strategies, the class will examine health care as a basic human right and analyze movements working towards eliminating disparities in health. Fulfills Pitzer social responsibility requirement.

course.title: Race Empire Filipnx America
course.description: Examines the interplay of historical, social, political, and cultural factors that have influenced, and continue to influence, the Filipin@ American experience in the U.S. Similarities and differences within the Filipin@ community ,as well as with other Asian American and ethnic/racial groups will be examined.

course.title: Senior Sem in Environ Analysis
course.description:
The EA senior seminar is organized around themes of climate catastrophe and conceptions of
our present and future. We examine philosophical premises about nature, culture, race, and
humanness that undergird perceptions of climate change, and we tackle how to deal with
climate catastrophe at personal and communal levels?as thinking, feeling, and justice-
oriented beings. This course requires readings, active discussion, and process-oriented
brainstorming and praxis work. We embody the principle of thinking through (and thinking
with) environmental problems by reading about the work of scholars and activists who
question anthropocentrism, and we create our own projections of what is to come. Our goal for
the class is to generate collective approaches for surviving and thriving even when the planet
is not/may not?this is what Donna Haraway calls ?cultivating conditions for ongoingness.?

course.title: AI & Land(scape) Representation
course.description: The Oxford Junior Dictionary has began replacing terms about nature with terms about technology. Elon Musk's Masterplan IV does not include the landscape except as a blank slate onto which electrical power and digital equipment co-occupies space with humans. Land transformed to landscape by jurisdiction and ownership and has perennially been used to represent ideas, sometimes in physical terms, sometimes as visual artifice. With digital media, multiple issues of representation arise. The landscape is the resource-rich setting of life. The compound urgencies of the moment create problems for its long-term sustainability. This is a problem-solving course that emphasizes critical observation and synthesis as it examines transdisciplinary solutions to complex problems represented in land(scape), the places where we dwell. Paradoxically, an area of knowledge not particularly well-comprehended by AI, it promises elegance of problem-solving. Hypothetically, can AI work in an hybrid format with conventional human-based analyses to meet the cultural and ecological imperatives of urgency?

course.title: Calculus I
course.description:
Introduction to the basic concepts of the calculus, including slopes,
rates of change, limits, the derivative and the integral, and the relationships between
these concepts, especially the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, with applications
to the natural and social sciences. Each concept will be treated from numerical,
analytic and geometric perspectives. Prerequisite: a grade of C or above in
Mathematics 23 or 25 or a satisfactory score on the mathematics placement
examination or permission of instructor.

course.title: Fndn Western Political Thought
course.description: An introductory lower-division course exploring major thinkers and movements in Western political theory. It surveys foundational ideas from ancient philosophers like Plato and Aristotle, modern theorists such as Marx and key Marxists, and contemporary figures including John Rawls and Robert Dahl. The course also incorporates critical and alternative perspectives from thinkers like Angela Davis, Carole Pateman, and Ursula K. Le Guin, examining how their insights challenge and expand the traditional canon in Western political thought.

course.title: Contemporary Democratic Theory
course.description: An upper-division political theory course focused on major contemporary models of democratic theory central to political science and political theory- such as Deliberative Theory, Dahl's Standard Theory, Schumpeter's Elite Theory, Participatory Theory, and Epistemic Theory. Students will explore key frameworks that define modern understandings of democracy, analyzing their assumptions, strengths, and limitations. The course then applies these theoretical models to real-world political debates and issues through detailed case studies, encouraging critical assessment of how democratic theories function in practice and shape contemporary political discourse.

course.title: Social Psychology
course.description: In this course, we will learn how social behavior is scientifically studied, the major topics and findings in the field, and how to apply social psychology to real-life situations. Specific topics include (but are not limited to) the self, emotion, relationships and attraction, stereotyping and prejudice, attitudes, and social influence. Satisfies: SOC

course.title: Senior Research Methods
course.description: This course will introduce students to the methods of conduction scientific research in the field of psychology. Theoretical, conceptual, and ethical issues as well was data-analytic strategies invovled in conducting research will be addressed. This course is designed for students who are interested in pursuing graduate studies in psychology.

course.title: Senior Research & Colloquium
course.description: A team-taught course intended to prepare students for subsequent work in Senior Thesis (THEA 191H PO) or Senior Project (THEA 192H PO). In Senior Colloquium, students choosing to write a traditional thesis will conduct research and write rough drafts. Students choosing to engage in a creative project will conduct research and carry out conceptual work and planning. The course seeks to create an intellectual and artistic community through the informal and formal sharing of work among class members and instructors. Letter grade only. Prerequisites: THEA188  PO or consent of the instructor.

course.title: Senior Thesis
course.description: A formal academic investigation of a theatrical topic, written under the close supervision of Theatre faculty members. The thesis process includes traditional and non-traditional research, submission of drafts for revision, a public informal research/poster presentation and a formal thesis defense. Letter grade only. Prerequisite: THEA 188 PO.

course.title: Repertory
course.description: Development of choreographic skill and/or performance quality and skill through choreographing or performing in dance faculty supervised productions. Does not meet fine arts breadth requirement. Half course, one dance, average of 4 hours of rehearsal per week.  May be taken twice for credit.  Eligibility by audition. Permission of instructor.

course.title: Gender & Sexuality in Erly Ameri
course.description:
In North America from the 1600s to the 1800s definitions of and beliefs about gender and sexuality were shaped by dynamic forces in geo-politics, social boundaries, and nascent, but coalescing cultural ideologies. Through analysis of primary sources and close readings of scholarly articles, monographs, and theory this course will explore the dynamic encounters between early modern communities where gender and sexuality were contested, negotiated, and redefined in an era of encounters, colonization, resistance, and revolution set the stage for the emergence of the United States and created patterns of thought and behavior that continue to influence the present. 

Rather than follow the narrative trajectory that chronicles European exploration and settlement leading into the creation of the United States, this course is divided into sections
that interrogate subject matter through both geographic spaces and specific historiographical problems. Particular emphasis will be given to borderlands and ?gender frontiers? across North America wherein diverse populations came into contact and through interaction, exchange, conflict, and accommodation shaped and re-shaped meanings, practices, and performances of gender and sexuality.

course.title: Poetry, Form and Process
course.description: This creative writing seminar, geared toward poetry, introduces students to experimental and constraint-based forms, including procedural, ritual, conceptual, and durational writing. We will look how authors use constraint and experiment to expand the field of the possible, will borrow their methods to write poetry, and will develop constraint-based projects of our own. This course is a workshop course in whichstudents will write new poems every week and submit 3-4 poems to workshop with the class.

course.title: Directed Research in Psychology
course.description: This course is for a research practicum with a Psychology faculty member focusing on different aspects of scientific psychological research such as experiment design, data collection, literature review, data analysis, and conference presentation or manuscript preparation. This class differs from Independent Study in that the research must be part of the faculty member's continuous line of inquiry in that faculty member's research lab. Students may register in the class for either 0.25 credit (at least 5 hours of directed research per week; 8-10 page paper or equivalent academic work) or 0.5 credit (at least 10 hours per week; 15-20 page paper or equivalent). Students may register more than once in Directed Research. A maximum of 1 credit may accumulate to apply toward graduation (not major) requirements. Students may also enroll in PSYC197B for a non-credit option, in which case they do not complete the academic work required for academic credit.  Instructor Permission Required. High-Pass/Pass/No-Pass grading only.

course.title: Sociology of Education
course.description: This course is an introduction to the foundations of and current issues in the sociology of education. In this class, we will look at the structure, practices, content, and outcomes of schooling, in light of their relationships to the wider society in which schools are situated.  We will note the link between schools and societal stratification, discuss the outcomes of schooling and how these outcomes are produced, and consider sociological perspectives on contemporary education reforms. This class counts towards the Social Responsibility Praxis requirement. Over the course of the semester, students spend 40 hours working in partnership with a community organization on a culminating course project.

Students are responsible for an oral presentation on progress and plans in the first half of the thesis research.

course.title: History of Mexico
course.description: The course traces Mexican history from pre-Columbian times to the present. It explores the character of Indigenous societies, the nature of the encounter, the colonial legacy, the tumultuous nineteenth century, the Mexican Revolution, United States-Mexican relations, politics during the 20th century, immigration, the rise of social movements and the current drug war.

course.title: Health Psychology
course.description: This course is designed to provide students with an introduction to the growing field of Health Psychology. The course will assess core aspects of Health Psychology including theories contributing to the development of Health Psychology, the role of biospsychosocial processes and stress in health and illness, coping with chronic illness and pain, and the role of health behavior in prevention and treatment. It will also discuss a variety of psychosocial interventions and evaluate the relationship between behavior and factors such as diet, exercise, sleep, and stress as they pertain to health and illness. Course meets Social Science general education requirement.

course.title: Psychological Disorders
course.description: This course will focus on the description of abnormal behavior in human beings and the various theoretically based explanations for it, both past and present. Intervention strategies relevant to the prevention or reduction of psychological suffering due to different disorders will also be explored. Prerequisite: Psychology 52.

course.title: Introduction to Wheel Throwing
course.description: This course is an introduction to the techniques and concepts that constitute the contemporary vessel in ceramics. Topics covered include basic pottery wheel techniques: centering throwing, and trimming, in addition to conceptual development, firing, glazing, and ceramic history past and present. Classes will consist of technical demonstrations, lectures, slides, work time, and critiques.

course.title: Senior Thesis in Mathematics
course.description: Senior thesis offers the student, guided by the faculty advisor, a chance to experience a taste of the life of a professional research mathematician. The work is largely independent with guidance from the research advisor. The principal objective of the senior thesis program is to help you develop intellectually and improve your written and verbal communication skills.  Students are expected to present their work orally and to produce a thesis conforming to the publication standards of a professional mathematician. Prerequisite(s): Senior standing as a mathematics major and permission from the Mathematics Senior Thesis Coordinator.

course.title: Intro to Ceramic Sculpture
course.description:
ART 121 SC - Introduction to Ceramic Sculpture
This course is an introduction to contemporary sculptural practices in clay. Topics covered include hand-building techniques, conceptual development, firing, glazing, ceramic history, and contemporary artistic practices. Classes will consist of lectures, discussions, technical demonstrations, assignments, and critiques.

course.title: Intro to Modern U.S. History
course.description: How do we understand the past and why does it matter? Focusing on the period since the Civil War, this course introduces students to the interpretive work of history through analysis of primary documents and different historical arguments. Topics include the politics of Reconstruction, the growth of industrial society, reform and radicalism, imperialism and war, the Great Depression, race and ethnicity, civil rights, feminism, the student movement and the New Right.

course.title: Cross-Cultural Psychology
course.description: This course will focus on the study of how culture influences human behavior and psychological processes. Basic to understanding people and their development in different cultures is the knowledge of their values, beliefs, and attitudes. We will discuss different methods used in comparative studies and how these methodologies have enhanced our knowledge of similarities and differences especially how it relates to developmental processes. A main theme for this class is how psychological research conducted in Eurocentric settings do not often generalize to other cultures.  Between group differences and within group differences will also be discussed.

course.title: Environmental Geology
course.description: Investigates the complex interactions between humans and their geologic environment, including an introduction to essential geologic concepts, as well as studies of geologic resources, geologic hazards and the impact that humans have on geologic systems. Field trips.

course.title: Senior Literature Thesis
course.description: The senior capstone exercise for all chemistry majors is the Senior Thesis with two options:  literature thesis (CHEM191  PO) or experimental thesis (CHEM194  PO). The literature thesis in grant proposal format is based on literature research. The Senior Thesis experience focuses on further developing students' content knowledge and skills relevant to the professional chemist, including interacting with data and scientific literature, effectively communicating with a broader community of chemists, taking ownership of a project, and conducting oneself in a professional manner.

course.title: Senior Experimental Thesis
course.description: The senior capstone exercise for all chemistry majors is the Senior Thesis with two options:  literature thesis (CHEM191  PO) or experimental thesis (CHEM194  PO). The experimental thesis is based on original research in collaboration with a faculty member. The Senior Thesis experience focuses on further developing students' content knowledge and skills relevant to the professional chemist, including interacting with data and scientific literature, effectively communicating with a broader community of chemists, taking ownership of a project, and conducting oneself in a professional manner.

course.title: Hip Hop Music Video & Film
course.description:
Course examines Hip Hop music video and film as dynamic sites of visual, sonic, and lyrical aesthetics through Kendrick Lamar and co-director Dave Free (The Little Homies), in collaboration with choreographer Charm La'Donna's manipulation of space and movement as expressive beats, bars, and flow.

Course focuses on formal analysis of Lamar's six albums and music videos (2011-2025) and his Super Bowl Halftime Show, exploring intertextuality, sampling, and visual storytelling. Students analyze iconography, symbolism, poetic metaphor, sonic texture, and elements of mise-en-scène, and rhythmic editing across music videos, short and feature-length films, and live performance.

Historical context traces Hip Hop sampling from blues, jazz, funk, soul, and R&B, examining the genre's transformation of the 9 Elements and 4 Principles. Drawing on perspectives from video essayists, journalists, podcasters, and rappers, students study Hip Hop Kulture in dialogue with art, cinema, and global media.

course.description: This course is for a research practicum with a Psychology faculty member focusing on different aspects of scientific psychological research such as experiment design, data collection, literature review, data analysis, and conference presentation or manuscript preparation. This class differs from Independent Study in that the research must be part of the faculty member's continuous line of inquiry in that faculty member's research lab. Students may also enroll in PSYC197A with the option for credit.  Instructor Permission Required. High-Pass/Pass/No-Pass grading only.

course.title: Intro to Sociocultural Anth
course.description: Study of the structure and dynamics of human culture and social institutions from a comparative perspective. Diversity in ways of life and patterns of social organization explored through ethnographic materials from societies around the world.

course.title: Food, Memory, and Community
course.description:
Food, Memory, and Community: Everyday Practices of Resistance

This course explores food in Latin America as a site of memory, identity, and power. Through topics such as migration, Indigenous foodways, and community-based practices, students examine how everyday food practices reflect inequality while also sustaining culture, resilience, and collective care.

course.title: Senior Thesis
course.description: Senior Thesis. An independent research project culminating in a thesis at least 30 pages in length written in the Spanish under the guidance of a department faculty member and read by one additional reader. Year-long course, half-credit per semester; grade and credit awarded upon completion at the end of the second semester.

course.title: Public Policy Process
course.description: What is public policy and who makes it? The course has two parts: Theories of the Policy Process and Practical Applications for Future Policymakers. It thus focuses on both the ?why? and the ?how? of government?s role in addressing perceived public problems associated with the American political and policy landscapes. In the first part we examine the major theories, frameworks, concepts, and substantive issues surrounding the study of public policy and the policymaking process. In the second part we will study a range of policy issues, including economic and social policy, national defense and veterans? affairs, health and education, as well as immigration and homelessness. This is a survey course well-suited for upper-level politics students interested in the policy studies subfield of political science, as well as students interested in learning about contemporary public policy challenges.

course.title: American Grand Strategy
course.description: This course examines the state of American Grand Strategy in the 21st century. Scholars have debated the "competing visions for U.S. grand strategy" for decades. Indeed, American grand strategy in theory and practice begins with an appreciation for the United States' grand strategic ends: to ensure American liberty, security, and prosperity. But how should the nation achieve these ends? Engagement? Retrenchment? Critics argue that primacy is too costly, neo-isolationism is too risky, and selective engagement is not very selective. But as the North Atlantic Treaty Organization comes under increasing pressure from the United States, is collective security still viable? This all comes against the backdrop of increased adversary alignment as relations between Russia, China, North Korea, and Iran strengthen. This course will interrogate the state of American Grand Strategy as the United States celebrates 250 years of independence and offer a strategic outlook for the future.

course.title: Badminton
course.description: This class is open to badminton players of all levels.  Beginners will receive basic instruction that will allow them to understand the fundamentals and rules of the game.  They will be provided with a comfortable, low-pressure environment to grow as players, get some exercise, and learn to enjoy the game.

course.title: Senior Paper
course.description: This course is structured as a workshop designed to guide students through the creation of an independent, research-driven capstone paper in Spanish. Students will draw upon knowledge from prior coursework to develop and refine a research question, conduct in-depth investigation using primary and secondary sources, and produce a formal thesis. Emphasis is placed on the writing process, peer review, and research presentations, as well as critical discussions of methodologies and theoretical frameworks within Hispanic literature, cultural studies, and/or linguistics.

course.title: Structural Geology
course.description: A study of the formation of rock structures from microscopic to continental scale. Topics include stress, strain, deformation mechanisms and the large-scale forces responsible for crustal deformation. Field trip. Letter grade only. Prerequisites: One course from GEOL 121 PO , GEOL 125 PO, GEOL 127 PO, GEOL 129 PO, and GEOL 131 PO. Corequisites: A second course from GEOL 121 PO , GEOL 125 PO, GEOL 127 PO, GEOL 129 PO, and GEOL 131 PO.

course.title: Digital Fabrication in Fine Art
course.description: This intermediate level art course will explore digital fabrication within the realm of contemporary art. Assignments will encourage the integration of emerging methods such as 3D printing with traditional techniques such as moldmaking, casting, and other sculptural or expanded studio practices. Through presentations, independent research, critiques, and hands-on studio work, students will be exposed to a diverse array of artistic approaches and methodologies that merge analog and digital. Course satisfies Fine Arts general education requirement.

course.title: Beyond the Boundaries
course.description: Beyond the Boundaries: The U.S.-Mexico Borderlands since World War II. This course introduces students to the modern history of the U.S.?Mexico Borderlands by placing migrants and everyday people at the center of the story. Rather than treating large-scale economic and political changes as abstract forces, we examine how individuals living in and moving through the region experienced and reshaped these transformations in their daily lives. Course meets Social Science and Race and Ethnic Studies general education requirements.

course.title: Integrated Sci Research I
course.description: In this 0.25-credit course, students will gain experience working independently on an Integrated Sciences research experience, which may involve field, laboratory, or computational research (or any combination thereof) and will be mentored by a KDIS faculty member.  The format and expectations of the research will be mutually agreed upon at the start of the semester and must include an end-of-semester deliverable (e.g., reflection paper, oral or poster presentation, lab notebook, dataset, etc.). This course is a 0.25-credit course with a minimum of a 3-hour commitment each week. The course is taken as pass/fail. A total of at most 1 credit may accumulate in SCI196 and SCI197 towards graduation. The course may not be counted toward major requirements. In any semester, students may take only one Integrated Sciences Research course at KDIS.  Prerequisite: Permission of instructor

course.title: International Economic Relations
course.description: The principles and theories of international trade and finance in historical context. Topics include the bases for international trade in comparative advantage and economies of scale, foreign direct investment, immigration, trade policies and related political economy issues, foreign exchange markets, balance of payments accounting and the national income and product accounts, macroeconomic policies in an open economy, monetary union, international monetary systems, and financial crises. Does not count for Economics major or minor credit. Letter grade only. Prerequisites: ECON 051  PO.  Previously offered as ECON113  PO.

course.title: Sr Thesis: Humanities Major
course.description: Fall enrollment for a one-semester thesis, or a two-semester thesis. Enroll for HMSC192 SC in the spring for a two-semester thesis.

course.title: Computer Science Colloquium
course.description: Colloquium presentations and discussions of topics in computer science and closely related disciplines. For junior Computer Science majors only. Prerequisites: CSCI 051A PO, or CSCI 051G PO, or CSCI 051J PO, or CSCI 051P PO. P/NP grading only.

course.title: Women and Politics in America
course.description: This course analyzes the history of American women in political life from the mid-nineteenth century to the present. Following a historical chronology, we will explore the long struggle for womenâ¬"s suffrage, the work of reformers and radicals in the early twentieth century, the Black civil rights movement, feminism and anti-feminism, women as candidates and officeholders, and struggles for racial justice today.

course.title: Syntactic Analysis
course.description: This course examines the sentence structure of natural language, addressing the (mostly unconscious) knowledge people have about language and proposing cognitive structures for that knowledge. For example, we explain why you can run up a bill and run up a hill, but while you can run a bill up, you can't run a hill up. Over the course of the semester we will adjust our theoretical model of syntax (using the framework of generative syntax), arriving at a set of claims about the nature of syntactic structures that are universal to all languages. The course emphasizes analysis and argumentation, with a writing-centric curriculum. Letter grade only. Prerequisites: LGCS 010  PO or equivalent.

course.title: Thesis in Environmental Analysis
course.description: Senior Thesis in Environmental Analysis. Same as 191, but taken in both semesters of the senior year for half-credit each semester; grade and credit awarded at the conclusion of the second semester.

course.title: Integrated Sciences I-B
course.description: This course is normally taken concurrently with SCI030LA CM. These two courses emphasize how the integration of core concepts from chemistry and physics, and the use of both experimental and computational methods, are necessary to explore themes of health, brain, and planet. For example, the concepts of intermolecular forces and fluid mechanics are necessary to understand viscous flow in both water infrastructure and the human circulatory system. Combined, the concurrent courses include a total of 6 hours of lecture and 6 hours of lab per week. Prerequisites: SCI 010L CM and MATH 030 CM or higher

course.title: Foundations of Leadership
course.description: This course is designed to provide a solid foundation on how leadership is defined, viewed, and studied.  Using multidisciplinary approaches, the course will review conceptualizations and theories of leaders and leadership from ancient times to the present.

course.title: Individual Instruction, Level I+
course.description: Individual Instruction, Level I+. Half-hour lesson weekly.

course.title: Electronic Music Composition
course.description: An introduction to the creative synthesis and manipulation of sound on a computer, including signal processing, analog emulation and digital synthesis, and digital audio workstation software. Assignments will include compositions using these tools and exploration of works from the history of electronic music, though no musical background is required.

course.title: Languages for Religious Studies
course.description: This course offers an introduction to the writing system, pronunciation, and foundational grammar, syntax, and morphology of the target language. Emphasis on reading and translating texts of beginner-level difficulty. Course has language pre-requisistes.

course.title: Languages for Religious Studies
course.description: This course solidifies the basic linguistic principles covered in RLST 195L (or equivalent), develops familiarity with specialized vocabulary, complex sentence structures and ideas, identifies and explains linguistic irregularities, and, where appropriate, notes regional or dialectical variations. Emphasis on reading and translating texts of intermediate-level difficulty. Course has language pre-requisistes.

course.title: Econometrics I
course.description: An introduction to the application of multiple regression techniques for testing and evaluating economic theory. Topics include hypothesis testing, model specification, heteroskedasticity, and serial correlation. Extensive use is made of computers for data handling and estimation. Prerequisites: ECON101 CM or ECON102 CM, and some form of statistics: ECON120 CM, GOVT055 CM, PSYC109 CM. Students who complete ECON125 CM may not subsequently enroll in lower-level statistics courses.

course.title: Sem in Conserving Biodiversity
course.description: Recent studies estimate that as many as 10-50% of all species on Earth are at risk of extinction. Ongoing threats such as catastrophic climate change and pervasive human footprints through agricultural land use or resource exploitation pose major challenges to sustaining biodiversity. Ultimately, the threats facing species and ecosystems are driven by human behaviors and societal decisions alongside ecological processes. Finding solutions therefore requires inter-disciplinary theories, concepts, and skills. This course will introduce students to a broad range of techniques that are relevant to conservation biology and science ranging from mathematical biology to community ecology to the social sciences. The course will be centered on discussions and collaborative group work. Prerequisite: BIOL 041E PO.

course.title: Intro to Film
course.description:
Film and video are often considered to be a distinct semiotic
system or art form with their own language. This course surveys the variety of
structures which can organize moving pictures: from Hollywood continuity editing,
Soviet montage and cinema verite to voice-over documentary, talking heads and
postmodern voices with no center at all. The course includes silent film, classic
Hollywood narrative, avant-garde film and video, documentary and activist video.
Enrollment is limited.

course.title: Environmental Futuring
course.description: This course is an elective course for the major in Environmental Analysis. It explores the politics of environmental futuring across diverse histories and geographies. Drawing on works in interpretive social sciences, we examine existing and emerging efforts that shape present-day and future human-environment interactions to ensure sustainability and resilience, and how these discourses and practices create and sustain new forms of power and agency. We interrogate the socio-cultural and ethical implications of key policy issues, including rural and urban ecology, agricultural and industrial pollution, human rights-based environmental activism and litigation regarding water and oil, extinction prevention and rehabilitation, and public health. This discussion-based, seminar-style course will empower you with analytical tools and comparative sensitivities to engage in informed discussions about sustainable and resilient futures.

course.title: Stage Combat
course.description: Students are introduced to the concentrated study of basic unarmed stage combat techniques. The focus of this study helps develop the actor's awareness of body, movement, partnering, consent and safety. The course culminates in the creation and execution of a choreographed unarmed fight scene.

course.title: Senior Project
course.description: A two-semester directed study of selected topics, culminating in a broad-ranging research paper or translation with contextual commentary and critical analysis. Letter grade only. Prerequisites: CHIN111B PO.

course.title: Codes
course.description: Students will learn foundational principles in the sciences, experimental methods, as well as data science and computer science concepts for scientific insight, including Python programming. No prior science or computing experience is expected.

course.title: Colonial Latin America
course.description: Examines the rise of the Aztec and Incan empires; the Spanish conquest and settlement of the Americas; the evolution and consolidation of colonial institutions; the significance of race, gender and sexuality in shaping the culture of the colonial society from the perspectives of Indigenous, European and African peoples; and the settlement of Brazil and the impact of the Age of Revolution, especially the Haitian Revolution, on the process of independence. (Core course, Latin America and the Caribbean)

course.title: Radical Care
course.description:
The recent pandemic made all the more visible a powerful fact: we are in the midst of a global ?crisis of
care.? The growing inequalities produced by late capitalism have disrupted our social capacities for
everything from birthing and raising children to caring for friends and family to maintaining households
and communities. And yet such reproductive labor is essential for the creation and maintenance of social
bonds and the functioning of institutions and infrastructures. How are artists and activists pushing back
against this crisis, forging collective movements that view ?care? for one?s self and one?s community as
moral imperatives to act? How might the expression of radical care?in literature, activism, and art?call
into being more socially just relations among friends, family, neighborhoods, and transnational
communities? We will read recent scholarship on the philosophy, sociology, and politics of care to enter
and transform debates on a wide range of issues, including mutual aid, the prison abolition movement,
feminism, care work, and public health.

course.title: Introduction to Sociology
course.description: This course examines introductory concepts and theories in the study of Sociology. Attention is given to sociological theory, inequality of race, class, gender, and sexuality, white privilege, as well as power, authority, and movements for social change.

course.title: College Campus Culture in Lit
course.description: Historically, the university is a funny place where modern ideas of professional accomplishment collide with medieval philosophies of higher learning. American college campuses, especially, have also been a petri dish for radical activism and social change in the U.S., even as the institutions themselves operate according to generations-old traditions. It is an intense 4 years, but most U.S. college graduates still remember their undergraduate days as a uniquely transformative period in their lives and continue to identify with their alma mater decades after their last day of attendance. Together, we will read texts that explore the wonderfully weird experience of college life, use our writing to tease out the significance of college to us, and take stock of how our time at college has transformed us on and off the page.

course.title: Special Topics in Government
course.description:
Topics change with each offering. The topic for Fall 2026 will be "Public Policy in the Age of AI".

Artificial intelligence is reshaping how we live, work, and govern. There is extreme uncertainty over where this revolution will take us. Are we entering an era of rapid economic growth? Are we creating uncontrollable superintelligence spelling humanity?s doom? Is this all one big speculative bubble awaiting market correction? Beneath these questions are foundational policy dilemmas related to how AI will reshape national security, intellectual property, labor, education, civil liberties, energy production, and more. This course will thrust students to the edge of those debates and expose them to the policy battles happening right now at all levels of government. Prerequisites: GOVT020  CM or the equivalent.

course.title: Introduction to Sociology
course.description: Introduction to Sociology. Characteristics of groups, institutions, society and culture. Social interaction, self-image, status. Brief consideration of social change, ethnicity, the urban environment and demography. Course is equivalent to SOC 001  PZ.

course.title: Introduction to Sociology
course.description: Introduction to Sociology. Characteristics of groups, institutions, society and culture. Social interaction, self-image, status. Brief consideration of social change, ethnicity, the urban environment and demography. Course is equivalent to SOC 001  PZ.

course.title: Medicalization of Social Life
course.description: This course will explore the phenomenon of medicalization, or the process by which more and more of social life and human behavior have come to be understood and governed through medical categories. Readings will be derived from empirical sociology, intellectual history, and critical social theory including the likes of Ilich, Foucault, and Agamben. Policy responses to the coronavirus pandemic will be highlighted as an especially salient case study of medicalization.

course.title: Environmental Justice
course.description:
There is a small but growing movement in the United States which contends that environmental harm is distributed in a fundamentally racist manner. What does this mean and how do we adjudicate such claims? 

This course will critically examine the Environmental Justice (EJ) movement in the United States: its history, central claims, frameworks and methods for analyzing race, class and the environment, EJ campaigns, and on-going strategies. 

In this course, you will actively learn to analyze environmental issues using an environmental justice lens, evaluate the race and equity implications of environmental harms, and be inspired to do something about environmental injustice!

This course fufills the SRX Pitzer educational objective

course.title: Philosophical Questions
course.description: In this course we will examine a set of philosophical questions drawn from the history of philosophy, including but not limited to the following: What is the nature of reality? Does God exist? What is the relation between mind and body? Do we really know anything? What is knowledge? What makes you the same person over time? What is cultural relativism? Do we have free will, or are our actions determined? What is a conspiracy theory?  We will investigate these topics through the writings of ancient, medieval, modern, and contemporary philosophers. In addition, the seminar is designed to develop students? critical thinking and to help them construct and analyze philosophical claims and arguments with clarity and insight.

course.title: La Familia
course.description: In this seminar, we will explore varying conceptions and constructions of ?la familia? (the family) among Latinx people living in the U.S.  We will examine la familia from a comparative perspective, across different Latinx groups, within families, and in relation to immigration status and migration journeys. We will also consider the psychological, sociocultural, and political factors that contribute to the complexity and diversity of Latinx families.  We also consider intersecting experiences of students who are the first in their families to attend college, those for whom English is not their first language, and individuals who have attended under-resourced schools.  Through research and reading first-hand narrative accounts, we will explore how migration experiences, educational opportunities and barriers, and family dynamics intersect to influence relationships among family members, educational trajectories, and well being.

course.title: The Room Where it Happens
course.description:
The Room Where it Happens: The Politics of Musical Theater

This course considers the relationship between musical theater and politics, broadly defined.  Through an in-depth analysis of several shows, songs and scenes, we will use musical theater as a lens through which to explore abiding themes in political science including power, protest, social justice, freedom, identity, representation, and governmental design.  Throughout the course we will reflect on such questions as: what makes a composition, performance or production ?political?? How does art both reflect and shape political culture? How are music and theater used to mobilize or marginalize?

course.title: Caribbean Beyond Reggae/Beaches
course.description:
The Caribbean Beyond Reggae Music and Beaches
When many people think of the Caribbean, images of white-sand beaches, all-inclusive resorts, and reggae rhythms dominate. This seminar challenges those tropes and invites students to explore the complex histories, cultures, languages, and politics of the Caribbean. This seminar explores the art of epistolary writing?the crafting of letters?as a means to deepen both writing skills and cross-cultural understanding. Students will engage in an ongoing correspondence with peers in Guadeloupe (French Caribbean island), exchanging letters that reflect on assigned readings about the Caribbean while also fostering dialogue about lived experiences, student life, and cultural perspectives. This seminar is all about discovering the power of letter writing?not just as a way to practice your writing, but as a bridge to another world. Throughout the semester, you will exchange letters with a pen pal in Guadeloupe. Together, you?ll reflect on the books we read about the Caribbean, while also asking questions and learning about your pen pal?s daily life, studies, and culture. By the end of the course, you?ll become a stronger writer, a deeper thinker, and a more empathetic communicator! This process will challenge students to write with clarity, empathy, and purpose, while encouraging curiosity and respectful inquiry into the lives of others. In the seminar students will have the immense honor and opportunity to be lectured by Caribbeanist faculty and writing experts across Claremont colleges and disciplines.

course.title: Hauntology:Ghsts, Spctrs, Spirts
course.description:
Hauntology: Ghosts, Specters, and Spirits
This course explores the cultural politics of haunting and being haunted. Drawing on classic and contemporary works in anthropology, we examine culturally particular, historically situated experiences and interpretations of ghostly and other supernatural encounters and how they shape political subjectivities and agencies. Specifically, we interrogate how embodied episodes, such as spirit possession and trance, afford social actors unique opportunities for political articulation, expression, and imagination in various contexts of domination, oppression, and violence. This discussion-based and seminar-style course will provide you with anthropological concepts and historical sensibilities to think about and relate to ghosts, specters, and spirits differently.

course.title: Labor and the Good Life
course.description: When you leave college, you?ll embark on a lifetime of work. In this course, at the start of your Pitzer journey, we will think about labor from a variety of disciplinary perspectives, asking about the definition(s) of ?work? itself, the politics of employment, and questions like how work can contribute to (or detract from) a life well lived. Your work will be cut out for you: the seminar will be heavily discussion-based, with course materials ranging from scholarly articles, to popular essays, to works of theater and film.

course.title: To Live & Die in LA: Latinx Amer
course.description:
To Live and Die in L.A. (Latinx America)
This course explores Latinx American fictions situated in or emerging from Los Angeles/ Southern California. By looking at short stories, poetry, novels, art, film and mixed media, the course provides an overview of the many voices, perspectives and stories from a variety of Latinx writers, artists and thinkers that have shaped the rich history of Latinx literature in this geopolitical region. From humorous and playful approaches to living in the city, to poignant stories of survival and resistance, this class offers a glimpse into the long trajectory of Latinx American writers who speak on what it means (in reference to 2pac?s poetic approach) to live and die in LA.

course.title: Living in a Biodiversity Hotspot
course.description: If asked to name a place rich in biological diversity, many people on our campuses might think of somewhere far away, maybe the Amazon or Madagascar. Yet like the Amazon, the Claremont Colleges are part of what ecologists call a biodiversity hotspot. What makes this place a biodiversity hotspot? What benefits, challenges, and responsibilities might come with living in a hotspot? This seminar explores these questions through readings, guest speakers, and field trips. We will use journaling to incubate ideas, then develop articles with the goal of engaging ourselves and others in our community more deeply with the local environment.

course.title: AI and Society: Conversations
course.description:
AI and Society: Conversations for a Humanistic Future
This course is grounded in three things: the sociological imagination; an embrace of deeply humanistic questions; and the belief that we have individual and collective agency in how we respond to the ?polycrisis? we are living through. Artificial intelligence ? and the uncritical rush to incorporate it ? is an emergent transformative process that intersects with massive inequality, anti-democratic political agendas, climate change and much more. Rather than passively accepting an AI-shaped future, this course is an invitation to participate in some critical and humanistic conversations about its pitfalls and possibilities. How does the rising tide of AI integration shape education, work, social life, political culture, and more? What of its manifestations do we want to accept, refuse or revise? What new norms and practices do we want to forge, as we make a future together through our daily and weekly lives with others?

course.title: Experiments in Media Art
course.description: For the last hundred years, artists all over the world have used the moving image and sound for experiments that bear little relation to more familiar forms of commercial cinema.   Sometimes called "avant-garde cinema,? ?experimental film,? or ?critical cinema,? these movies ask us to question what a film is and what a film can do.  Through close viewing, discussion, group exercises, and writing, this class will analyze some of the experimental approaches to cinema.

course.title: Brazil through Films
course.description:
Brazil through Films: A Cinematographic Look at Old and Modern Social Issues 
Brazil is often imagined through celebratory images of racial mixture, cultural vibrancy, and national unity, yet its history has also been shaped by colonization, Indigenous dispossession, slavery, regional inequality, authoritarianism, urban segregation, and persistent struggles over race, class, gender, labor, and land. In this course, we will examine major social problems in Brazil through film, from the colonial period to the present. By pairing films with historical and critical readings, we will explore how cinema represents social crisis, whose perspectives it privileges, and how filmmakers interpret the past and present of Brazilian society. Through our readings, screenings, and discussions, we will analyze topics such as slavery and resistance, post-abolition racism, land inequality, dictatorship and political repression, urban poverty and violence, domestic labor, and contemporary Indigenous and democratic struggles. We will work on and strengthen our ability to write clear, well-supported arguments for different audiences through drafting, revision, peer review, and constructive feedback.

course.title: Dreaming of Infrastructure
course.description: This class offers a creative introduction to the study of infrastructure. Understanding infrastructures as the material conditions for life in common, we will consider the way these foundations produce different experiences for different populations, ordering the world and its resources in service of particular political projects. From the building of the transcontinental railroad and the Panama Canal to the contemporary proliferation of data centers, students will be challenged to think through the historical implications of built environments and the futures these structures imagine.

course.title: The Ancient World and Us
course.description:
The Ancient World and Us: Greeks, Romans, and Egyptians from antiquity to today 
The ancient Mediterranean world?famous as the home of ancient Egyptians, Greeks, and Romans?was in fact inhabited by millions of people who spoke hundreds of languages and worshipped countless gods over thousands of years. Today, that region encompasses some 40 modern countries and the cultural influence of the ancient Mediterranean is felt around the world. In this seminar, we explore ancient Greek, Roman, and Egyptian culture from the starting points of ancient literature, art, and architecture and explore how the their world has been imagined, constructed, and re-invented in art, literature, and historical narratives in later periods (including modern art, contemporary novels, and pop culture).

course.title: Human Nature in Science Fiction
course.description: Since Mary Shelly?s Frankenstein (The Modern Prometheus), science fiction has become a substantial, and popular, vein of literature. In this course, we will explore a range of science fiction works with attention on how they portray what it is to be human. Specifically, we will examine certain questions like: What defines science fiction? In what ways does it adhere to and depart from science? How is it used as a tool for communication of human values and flaws? And, to what degree can it predict future societal directions? Works examined in the course will include those by Octavia Butler, Ursula Le Guin, Frank Herbert, Kazuo Ishiguro, Isaac Asimov, and Ted Chiang. The course will also involve some analysis of film inspired by science fiction. Class discussions will provide a platform for assignments that develop analytical, argumentative writing skills.

course.title: Escaping Religion
course.description: Apostasy, deconversion, the loss of faith. How do these things happen? This course will look at how and why people reject religion.

course.title: Radical & Countercultural Media
course.description: Through a cultural studies framework, this course explores radical and countercultural media production. With a particular focus on queer and trans cultural production, students will analyze the aesthetics and reception of film, music, and other media to devise a critical framework for understanding gender, race, sexuality, class, and ability in developing liberatory politics.

course.title: Histories of Health & the Enviro
course.description:
Histories of Health and the Environment
What is the relationship between health and the environment in human history? How have humans shaped the physical environment, and how have environmental conditions affected human health and well-being? This seminar explores these questions from a historical perspective. We?ll focus on the history of environmental change in North America in the late eighteenth century though the twentieth century, considering historical processes in a global, comparative framework. We will examine the intersection of histories of the environment, health, and disease, with an emphasis on the reciprocal relationship between ecological change and human health outcomes. Human-induced ecological transformations have shaped patterns of health and disease, manifested in a multitude of dimensions, influencing cultural, social, economic, and geopolitical developments. In this course, we?ll study the history of anthropogenic environmental impacts alongside non-human, biological processes.

course.title: Politics & Literature
course.description: American political science and American modernist literature came of age at the same time.  Yet they took radically different approaches to interpreting political life.  How might we reimagine contemporary American politics through a careful analysis of American modernism?  Readings may include Gertrude Stein, Sherwood Anderson, Zora Neale Hurston, William Faulkner, Robert Frost, Willa Cather, John Steinbeck, Belle Turnbell, and William Carlos Williams.

course.title: Can I Get A Witness?
course.description:
Can I Get A Witness? Regarding the Pain of Others
I?ve often struggled with the limitation of what?s deemed a literature of witness. How are we implicated in the aftermath of crimes we did not ourselves witness? How can we best carry their stories forward, without appropriating them, without unduly calling attention to ourselves, and without in turn, having their stories displaced by ours? This class will explore innovative interventions on ways of looking through works by Carmen Maria Machado, Cathy Park Hong, Fernanda Melchor and others. And developing our own witnessing practice?producing one original work of nonfiction that engages theories of witnessing, uses one original source, and exemplifies social responsibility with a community partner organization.

course.title: Keep Your Coins, We Want Change
course.description:
Keep Your Coins, We Want Change: Social Movements of the Inland Empire
Students will learn together about the many opportunities to be meaningfully engaged with local nonprofits and social movements surrounding Pitzer College and the region of the Inland Empire. This course will take an in-depth look at how to be effectively involved in the local community and practice critical strategies to create change locally while you are here for the duration of your academic career.  Students will be reading the works of bell hooks, Pierre Bordieu, Pitzer professors Dr. Tessa Hicks Peterson and Dr. Jose Calderon and exploring the theoretical frameworks including critical pedagogy, social capital, and asset-based community development. Pitzer?s commitment to social justice has been built throughout the years of connection, reciprocity, understanding, and the collective work of students, nonprofit organizations, and community scholars and leaders. Deeply connected to CASA Pitzer?s core partnerships (Critical Action + Social Advocacy) countless past students have become community leaders working for immigrant rights, immigrant youth, LGBTQIA communities, community gardens, equitable preschool partnerships, civic engagement, and a more just world.

course.title: Senior Thesis in Physics
course.description: Original experimental or theoretical investigations in physics undertaken in consultation with a faculty member. Projects may be initiated by the student or by a faculty member. Present faculty research areas include astrophysics, biophysics, optics, solid-state and low-temperature physics, general relativity, quantum mechanics, particle physics, geophysics, and soft matter physics. Students are responsible for an oral presentation on progress and plans in the first half of the thesis research.

course.title: US Politics: Resistnce & Transfr
course.description:
U.S. Politics: Resistance and Transformation

This discussion-based seminar is designed to explore the racialization of American democracy and politics. Despite the inclusive and egalitarian principles written in the U.S. Constitution, words like equality, liberty, and freedom were not universally applied. Exclusion was built into the fabric of American politics, and many of the inequalities we see today stem directly from this early framework.  Black people and other people of color have demanded inclusion and representation in American politics, which has broadened opportunities for all. This introductory course will explore the founding of American democracy and politics in a racially divided world, and the ways that minoritized people have broadened American democracy.

course.title: Data Science Ethics
course.description: Data science is rapidly becoming more powerful, and it is being used for a broad range of private and public purposes. For example, companies use it to manipulate the behavior of their customers, and governments use it in choosing policing policies. This course examines ethical issues that arise in the conduct and use of data science. For example, suppose that an algorithm designed for use in the criminal justice system is unintentionally biased against the members of a certain race. Does the moral responsibility for this fall on the designer, the designer's employer, and/or the government agencies using the algorithm?

course.title: Biochemistry
course.description: This course combines principles from organic chemistry, molecular biology, and physical chemistry to explore the molecular structures and chemical processes necessary for life. The structure and function of biomolecules will be applied to enzyme kinetics and catalysis, metabolic pathways, broader bioenergetics concepts, and regulation. The laboratory will provide experience with isolating and characterizing biological molecules in the context of discovery-based projects.   Prerequisites: SCI 031LA CM, SCI 031LB CM, and SCI 111L  CM.

course.title: Directed Research in Psychology
course.description: This course is for a research practicum with a Psychology faculty member focusing on different aspects of scientific psychological research such as experiment design, data collection, literature review, data analysis, and conference presentation or manuscript preparation. This class differs from Independent Study in that the research must be part of the faculty member's continuous line of inquiry in that faculty member's research lab. Students may register in the class for either 0.25 credit (at least 5 hours of directed research per week; 8-10 page paper or equivalent academic work) or 0.5 credit (at least 10 hours per week; 15-20 page paper or equivalent). Students may register more than once in Directed Research. A maximum of 1 credit may accumulate to apply toward graduation (not major) requirements. Students may also enroll in PSYC197B for a non-credit option, in which case they do not complete the academic work required for academic credit.  Instructor Permission Required. High-Pass/Pass/No-Pass grading only.

course.title: Directed Research in Psychology
course.description: This course is for a research practicum with a Psychology faculty member focusing on different aspects of scientific psychological research such as experiment design, data collection, literature review, data analysis, and conference presentation or manuscript preparation. This class differs from Independent Study in that the research must be part of the faculty member's continuous line of inquiry in that faculty member's research lab. Students may also enroll in PSYC197A with the option for credit.  Instructor Permission Required. High-Pass/Pass/No-Pass grading only.

course.title: Intro to Comparative Politics
course.description: This survey course introduces students to the field of comparative politics by investigating cross-national similarities and differences in politics, economies and societies through several illuminating empirical case studies and examines the strengths and weaknesses of comparative analysis as a methodological tool. Topics may include: the formation of states and nations; the evolution of democratic and non-democratic political regimes; political development and culture; the role of culture and religion in modern politics; policymaking; and modes of political participation and protest.

course.title: Modern US History Since 1877
course.description: This introductory course covers major themes in U.S. history from Reconstruction to the HIV/AIDS crisis in the 1980s. Across this period, we will trace how understandings of citizenshipâ¬and who was deemed a citizenâ¬changed over time. Is citizenship a narrow legal category focused on political privileges and responsibilities? Or is citizenship a broader and more ambitious idea that includes freedom of movement, bodily autonomy, health, and economic security? Major topics explored include racial segregation and inequality, immigration, labor activism, American empire building, the Progressive Era, the Great Depression and World Wars, the Civil Rights Movement, and the Counterculture of the 1960s.

course.title: Vice and Addiction in US History
Disability, Race, & the Bodymind
course.description: In this course we will explore the following questions: What does it mean to be labeled as deviant or abnormal? How are deviance and abnormality constructed by society? How are people living under these categories experiencing life? Can one conform to so-called "normality"? To think through these questions, we will do a close examination of cultural and historical formulations of "deviance" and "abnormality," particularly in the United States. This course engages contemporary Medical, Psychological, and Cultural Anthropology to help students identify the function and consequences of socio-cultural evaluations of "deviance" and "abnormality." We will unpack how race, class, gender, sexual orientation, and mental and physical ability play into each other and inform popular, academic, and institutional understandings of what it means to be deviant.

course.title: Women and Gender in Islam
course.description:
This course will introduce you to a multi-faceted understanding of women and gender issues in Islam, mainly in the Qur'an, the Islamic scripture. We will explore topics such as construction of gender and gender expectations in Islam, Qur'an and in other
Islamic sources as well as study critiques and interpretations by contemporary Muslim scholars and/or feminists. Course meetings Letters and Gender and Women's Studies general education requirements.

course.title: International Politics
course.description: This course offers a comprehensive introduction to the history and theory of international politics. The course is divided into three roughly equal-sized sections. The first section offers an introduction to the two philosophical/theoretical traditions in international relations thought: rationalism (and its realist and liberal variants) and social constructivism (and its statist and global variants). The second section covers a series of significant periods in international political history from the emergence of the modern system of states in Europe in the sixteenth century to the end of the Cold War. The third section investigates various issues in contemporary international politics.

course.title: Authoritarian Politics
course.description: There used to be a time when a similar course was often entitled, "regime change and democratization." In the ear of democratic backsliding, however, we examine the exact opposite of this once optimistic proposition that authoritarian regimes would eventually collapse and democratize. Instead, this course explores the core questions in authoritarian politics. What factors contribute to regime survival? What strategies do dictators deploy to stay in power despite social discontent and lack of accountability? To answer these questions, we draw on prominent theories, empirical research, and historical developments in China, the Middle East, former Soviet Union, and other non-democratic states.

course.title: The Art of Scientific Modeling
course.description:
This course is intended for students with little to no prior physics coursework who are interested in majoring in physics or astrophysics. This course will not be a crash course in AP physics content. Instead, we will focus on the far more important skill of creating quantitative models to test and analyze. A good scientific model starts out simple and is refined to better reproduce what we observe. We will use real data from in-class labs and demonstrations to create and test our models, and students will also learn how to properly analyze data and develop tools to test and refine models.

Prerequisites: Completion of or concurrent enrollment in MATH030 PO or equivalent.

course.title: Core Skills Workshop
course.description: Foundational quantitative skills are reinforced to prepare students for the HMC Core. Initial topics cover linear systems, logarithmic properties, and algebraic manipulation. Geometry and spatial reasoning are treated through similar triangles, right-triangle trigonometry, and vector decomposition on rotated axes. Differential and integral calculus concepts are reviewed, including rules for derivatives and integration techniques. These skills are then combined to solve multi-step problems from various STEM fields.
